results.title: ClarityCheck people-finder left millions of face photos exposed, likely without their knowledge
results.author: Ben Lovejoy
results.content:
ClarityCheck, a facial-identification tool for which it’s hard to think of many legitimate uses, reportedly left millions of face photos publicly exposed on the internet in a major privacy breach.
It’s likely that the vast majority of victims had no idea their photos had been uploaded to the site, and had never granted consent …
The service allows anyone to upload a photo of someone in order to carry out a reverse search of things like social media sites in order to identify them. ClarityCheck requires people to agree they have permission to upload the photo, but security researcher Jeremiah Fowler told Wired he was extremely skeptical about this.
He notes the service is explicitly designed for identification, and people don’t typically seek to identify themselves or people they [already] know.
The website has blog posts including Find Someone on Dating Sites by Email and How to Find Someone on Hinge (Even Without Matching).
Farrell told ExpressVPN that more than nine million image files uploaded to ClarityCheck were left publicly accessible on a cloud server for several months, noting that these were primarily facial images, though this included some duplication in the form of cropped and resized images.
I recently discovered a publicly exposed database that was neither password-protected nor encrypted. The database contained approximately 9,042,977 image files totaling 450.2GB of data. The exposed records consisted primarily of facial images stored in folders labeled “faces” and “profiles.” In a limited sample of the exposed images I reviewed as part of the investigation, I observed facial images of adults, teens, and children […]
Many of the uploaded images I saw may have originated from third-party sources such as private profiles, social media accounts, dating app accounts, screenshots, or physical photographs uploaded by third-party users.
He tracked the database to ClarityCheck, and the company acknowledged ownership and said it has now secured the data.
9to5Mac’s Take
One of the risks identified by Fowler is that the photos and their associated identities could be used by scammers to create fake social media posts intended to fool family and friends. A very common scam is to impersonate a family member in an emergency situation requiring immediate funds to be sent. Having access to face photos could certainly help facilitate this type of fraud.
We’ve previously outlined nine steps you can take to protect yourself against hackers and scammers.
Photo by Onur Binay on Unsplash
results.summary:
The facial-identification service ClarityCheck exposed over nine million user-uploaded photos on an unsecured cloud server, potentially compromising the privacy of adults, teenagers, and children worldwide.

### Key Points
- Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler discovered a database containing 9,042,977 image files totaling 450.2GB of data.
- The exposed files were neither password-protected nor encrypted, allowing public access to facial images for several months.
- ClarityCheck facilitates reverse image searches to identify individuals from social media profiles and dating apps without their consent.
- The company acknowledged ownership of the database and confirmed that the server has since been secured.
- Exposed data included images of minors, raising significant concerns regarding privacy and potential misuse by malicious actors.

### Why it Matters
This breach highlights the severe security risks associated with facial-recognition platforms that aggregate personal data without explicit user authorization. The exposure of these images provides scammers with high-quality assets to facilitate identity theft and sophisticated social engineering fraud.

results.title: MIT Economist Says H-1B Program Cripples Schooling for K-12 Kids
results.author: Neil Munro
results.content:
The H-1B visa program is draining the incentive for complacent politicians to fix the broken K-12 system used by many millions of ordinary Americans, says Daron Acemoglu, a famous economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
The educated elite “has given up on the education of Americans because they think that they can fill any skill gap with importing those skills [via the H-1B program], whether they are nurses, whether they’re doctors, whether they’re programmers. That’s the problem,” Acemoglu told Tyler Cowen, a zealously pro-migration economist at George Mason University.
Acemoglu is an ethnic Armenian who used the H-1B program to migrate from Turkey to the United States.
The Nobel Prize winner told Cowan:
I would love to have skilled immigration, but I would love also to renew the … social compact of America such that the influential people, be they politicians, journalists, or tech barons, really have a commitment to the education of Americans.
Cowen rebuked him, saying: “I don’t see that,” prompting the Turkey-born immigrant Acemoglu to respond:
Well, about half of people in the United States in middle school read and write a couple of grades below [below standards, and] we’re not doing anything about that despite the fact that everybody recognizes that we are moving into the skills age where we are going to need more and more human capital. We’re not doing anything. We’re just giving up on these people. I think that is what really bothers me, that somehow we have, as the most powerful, arguably the richest, country in the world, have resigned ourselves to give up on the education of about a third to a half of the youth.
“We’re throwing money at it, but we’re not really dealing with the root causes,” Acemoglu added.
Acemoglu’s comments infuriated Adam Ozimek, another pro-migration economist who works for pro-migration investors at the pro-migration Economic Innovation Group. He posted:
If you are looking for bad Acemoglu arguments, consider his criticism of skilled immigration, that it somehow is stopping us from improving the education of the bottom half or third of students???
Ozimek’s solution to the many civic, economic, and education problems caused by the H-1B and similar programs — described here — is to create more and bigger visa programs.
In June, an Indian-born investor and H-1B advocate suggested the program could help K-12 schools by steering Indian contract workers into Silicon Valley tech jobs so that U.S. tech graduates could be freed to teach kids in Alaska: “Dear Anti-immigrants constantly crying that foreigners are taking American jobs: Why aren’t you teaching in rural Alaska?”
The globalist Economist magazine is also slamming Acemoglu amid his populist shift:
Give an economist a few drinks, however, and some of them will venture their true opinions about this giant [Acemoglu]. “Much of his theoretical work is useful, but he uses his models to inform populist policies that have been tried before and failed,” blasts one well-known economist. Some commentators do not require Dutch courage. “I’ve been yelling about Acemoglu for literally a decade,” Noah Smith, an [pro-migration] economics blogger, has said, in response to a flurry of online criticism of Mr Acemoglu’s work.
Acemoglu’s new book, “What Happened To Liberal Democracy?” is surprisingly coy about migration’s economic impact on ordinary Americans. But on page 14, he spotlights the elite’s refusal to recognize the public’s opposition to migration: “Throughout the last several decades, about half the U.S. population has been concerned about immigration, especially illegal immigration … Mainstream politicians haven’t paid much attention to these concerns for most of this period.”
He is also shying away from mentioning immigration as he touts his new book. In an appearance on the Capitalisn’t streaming show, for example, he carefully avoided mentioning the 1924 immigration reform:
I don’t know of any example in history of sustained shared prosperity which works through anything other than sustained wage growth … That’s exactly what happened in the United States starting in early decades of the 20th century [after the 1924 immigration reform]. So much so that many companies … were sending their [hiring] agents all around the 50 states to find people that could work … because there was such a hunger for labor. It was that hunger for labor that was at the root of shared prosperity, and [the] disappearance of that hunger [is] due to technology, organizational changes, and other economic changes.
“Dems have ceased to be the workers’ party long ago, owing to their support for digital disruption, globalization, large immigrant flows, and ‘woke’ ideas,” he wrote in January 2025 after migration concerns allowed President Donald Trump to win the White House for a second time.
Acemoglu’s criticism of the H-1B program echoes the 2024 comments of another Nobel Prize-winning economist, British-born Angus Deaton, who recognized the many “Deaths of Despair” caused by government economic policies. Deaton wrote in 2024:
I also no longer defend the idea that the harm done to working Americans by globalization was a reasonable price to pay for global poverty reduction because workers in America are so much better off than the global poor …
I had also seriously underthought my ethical judgments about trade-offs between domestic and foreign workers. We certainly have a duty to aid those in distress, but we have additional obligations to our fellow citizens that we do not have to others.
Acemoglu’s comments also echoed May 2025 comments from Silicon Valley investor Marc Andreessen.
“If you’re a family… where I grew up [Wisconsin], and you’ve got a smart kid, and you think you’re going to get them into a top university in this country… there is no chance,” Andreessen told his rapt audience at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation. He added:
What level of untapped talent exists in this country that a combination of DEI and immigration have basically cut out of the loop for the last 50 years? And how long can we have this story to everybody in the Midwest and the South that says, “Sorry, because of historical oppression, your kids are SOL.”
For a decade, Breitbart News has carefully described the U.S. economic policy of Extraction Migration, including its impact on wages, productivity, and housing.
Breitbart News has also covered the white-collar visa-worker controversies, polls, and the civic impact as politicians subordinated citizenship to the priorities of investors and migrants.

MIT economist Daron Acemoglu argues that the H-1B visa program reduces political incentives to improve the American K-12 education system by allowing companies to bypass domestic skill gaps.

### Key Points
- Nobel laureate Daron Acemoglu claims elites prioritize importing foreign labor over investing in the education of American youth.
- Acemoglu notes that nearly half of U.S. middle school students currently perform below grade-level standards in reading and writing.
- Critics, including economist Adam Ozimek, argue that skilled immigration is not the primary cause of domestic educational failures.
- The debate highlights a growing divide among economists regarding the impact of migration on domestic wages and social mobility.
- Acemoglu’s perspective aligns with recent critiques from figures like Angus Deaton and Marc Andreessen regarding the neglect of the American workforce.

### Why it Matters
This debate highlights a fundamental tension between globalized labor strategies and the long-term development of domestic human capital. It suggests that reliance on visa programs may be masking systemic failures in the U.S. education system, potentially impacting future economic competitiveness and social stability.

results.title: ‘I Lost the Ability to Think’: The Mind-Control Drug Being Used to Rob Unsuspecting Tourists
results.author: Elisabeth Garber-Paul
results.content:
W hen the patient arrived, he was almost completely incoherent. The man’s assistant had found him unconscious earlier that evening and rushed him to the Clínica El Rosario hospital, where the man intermittently woke up in a delusional state — struggling to breathe, his heart pounding.
“He was not recognizing where he was,” says clinical toxicologist Juan Carlos Fernández. “It gave the impression that he was still under the effects of alcohol, that he was drunk. But the tests showed us there was no alcohol effect.”
The patient, an American professional who we’ll call Mark, would later explain how he ended up in that state to Fernández, who says he has permission to share the man’s story.
Fernández says Mark didn’t remember what happened after two much-younger women approached him late on a boozy Sunday night in December 2019. He said they met in Medellín, Colombia’s infamous Lleras Park, a tropical open-air plaza surrounded by bars where dozens of sex workers openly solicit clients. The two girls suggested they all go back to his nearby apartment, and Mark obliged. The doorman would admit he saw him entering with the pair. Two hours later, the women left. But nobody heard from Mark throughout the next morning and into the afternoon until the assistant found him and brought him to the hospital.
The doctors began to suspect he had been drugged with a substance called scopolamine, also known as Devil’s Breath.
Extracted from the seeds of the trumpet-shaped brugmansia flower — which blooms resplendent pinks, yellows, and whites across South America’s Andean regions — scopolamine is tasteless and odorless, and doses as small as 10 milligrams can induce a zombie-like state of compliance. When Mark came to, he discovered that his safe had been plundered for thousands of dollars in cash. Fernández’s theory is that Mark must have told the women the code to his safe in his pliant stupor.
A test showed no trace of scopolamine, but the drug is rapidly metabolized and is extremely difficult to identify even within a few hours after ingestion. Unlike some of the other substances used by Medellín’s burundangeras, women, some of whom are sex workers, who seduce men before drugging and robbing them, scopolamine “can lead to multiple organ failures and end in death,” Fernández says.
Two days after Mark was admitted to the hospital, he developed aspiration pneumonia. Fernández feared he might die. By then, Fernández was sure Mark had been drugged with scopolamine — no other drugs have such grave and particular effects.
Since the pandemic, tourism has exploded in Medellín as the onetime global murder capital and home of Pablo Escobar’s billion-dollar cocaine empire became a desirable global getaway. National Geographic named Medellín “one of the most inspiring places to visit in 2026” thanks to its natural beauty and bustling nightlife. Last year, more than 1.2 million tourists visited, up from less than 1 million in 2019, and the murder rate is at historic lows. However, it is increasingly a hub for international sex tourism. Adult sex work isn’t criminalized, and is highly visible in Medellín, where many American men and other foreigners come seeking to take advantage of the low prices for sex and lax age-of-consent laws.
“Sex tourism in Medellín has increased dramatically over the past decade,” says Jessica Van Meir, a Ph.D. candidate at the Harvard Kennedy School of Government studying the regulation of sex work in Latin America. “Passport-bro influencers promote Colombia” as a prime sex tourism destination, she says, stressing that it’s a small minority of the sex workers in the industry who drug and rob men.
Most of the American men who come here in search of sex workers leave unscathed, some wake up penniless — a few don’t wake up at all. Certain men have reportedly watched CCTV footage of their stupefied selves inexplicably helping their robbers gut their apartments of possessions. The same men — the victims are invariably men — then have a rude awakening when credit card statements reveal they have been taken on a drug-induced “million-dollar ride” through the city, stopping at every ATM on the way. Others become so docile they even transfer all of their savings from bank accounts and crypto wallets to their robbers. A few have died after their dates go awry, with 40 foreigners dying under mysterious circumstances in the city in 2023 alone.
Medellín is a “very happy, very open sort of place,” but that often lures foreigners into a false sense of security, says Alan Gongora, an American lawyer in Colombia whose firm has represented a number of victims of druggings, which are often perpetrated with drugs other than scopolamine. “This thing is very real,” he says. “It happens on a pretty regular basis.”
Now officials are scrambling to contain waves of druggings, robbings, and unexplained deaths involving foreign visitors. Police have launched targeted operations against criminal gangs of burundangeras, while increasingly barring entry to tourists they suspect are coming to the city primarily for sex tourism. Yet despite the crackdown, the attacks continue — and few outsiders understand how they actually happen.
SCOPOLAMINE ISN’T JUST A PROBLEM PARTICULAR to modern Medellín; its potential as a truth serum was inadvertently discovered more than a century ago. In the early 20th century, doctors gave women tiny amounts of the drug during childbirth to help induce a state of “twilight sleep.” Physicians observed people under the effects of scopolamine become particularly candid. In 1922, Dallas obstetrician Robert House tested the drug on two prisoners and made a convincing case that it was impossible to conceal the truth while under scopolamine’s influence. They “cannot create a lie … and there is no power to think or reason,” he wrote.
A 1922 news report on the experiment in the Los Angeles Record seemingly coined the phrase “truth serum,” according to a declassified 1993 CIA report. In the first half of the 20th century, some U.S. police forces may have used scopolamine “extensively,” per the CIA report.
During World War II, scopolamine was used on prisoners of war to swiftly extract information not only, according to legend, by the Nazi doctor Josef Mengele, but also by U.S. and U.K. intelligence services. The CIA then tested scopolamine during its MKUltra mind-control experiments in the 1950s. In 1963, the Supreme Court banned confessions given under scopolamine and other truth-inducers as unconstitutionally coerced.
Scopolamine was first used by criminals in Colombia in the 1970s, according to toxicologist Camilo Uribe, formerly a consultant to the country’s anti-narcotics police. It swiftly developed a reputation for producing a state of chemical hypnosis. “I can give you a gun and tell you to go kill someone and you will do it,” Uribe has said of scopolamine’s effects. Until the late 1990s, scopolamine was responsible for the majority of such druggings, but thieves learned it can make some people agitated and aggressive, complicating their efforts to rob them. Today, other drugs are more often deployed, chiefly benzodiazepines or the benzodiazepine Clonazepam, which also render a person zombie-like and more reliably submissive. Still, sometimes these drugs are combined with scopolamine. “Out of every 10 to 15 cases that enter emergency services, two or three may be a mixture of scopolamine with a tranquilizer,” says Uribe.
Scopolamine also has legitimate applications, and has been used to treat nausea and as palliative care for Parkinson’s patients. Some people even enjoy minute quantities as a recreational drug. Shamans, meanwhile, are known to consume the plant “to walk between worlds.”
Legitimate or otherwise, scopolamine is usually administered as a powder and is almost always dissolved in liquids. It blocks neurotransmitters regulating the flow of information to the part of the brain that records short-term memories, meaning that what happens after one has been “scopolamined” is not noted. “Scopolamine has a very short detection window,” says psychotherapist Augusto Pérez Goméz, a former member of a Colombian government commission on drug use, so instances of people being dosed with the drug often go unreported.
No matter which compound is actually used, many people in Colombia refer to these drugging-robberies as being “scopolamined.” But men trying to make sense of a night that has slipped clean out of memory — along with all their money — may find sympathy hard to come by.
“There is a group of people who, for me, are not tourists, they are sick and we must chase them wherever they are from,” Medellín Mayor Federico Gutiérrez said in 2024, highlighting the foreign tourists who come to Colombia to have sex with underage girls, after a Miami man was sentenced last year to life in prison for sexually abusing more than 50 minors after paying a local sex trafficker. In another widely-reported case in 2024, which led to a temporary city ban on sex work in Lleras Park, an Ohio man was found in a luxury hotel with two girls aged 12 and 13.
Gutiérrez acknowledged that drugging with scopolamine is a serious issue, but warned: “People go looking for what they should not be looking for.” And he called for Medellín not to be stigmatized: “It’s a beautiful city that has overcome some difficult times.”
ON A TUESDAY EVENING IN FEBRUARY, I’M looking out over Lleras Park, a botanical oasis and center of the city’s sex industry. Dozens of women mill about beneath exotic trees to sell their services. It’s early, but a handful of men are already fraternizing with them, asking for their prices and what they would be prepared to do in return. Some of the girls are clearly underage, but the police officers nearby do not appear interested in asking them to prove their identities.
A tall, beautiful woman in a leopard-print catsuit blows me a kiss and motions for me to come over. She introduces herself as Camila and says she is from Colombia’s northern Caribbean coast. After exchanging pleasantries, she tells me: “Amor, hay un hotel donde podemos ir. (My love, there is a hotel where we can go).” An hour would be $110. Two would be $190, and the entire night would be $270. “We’re going to have a great time,” she assures me. “We can do todo.” In Spanish, I ask her if she might scopolamine me. She laughs and pushes me playfully in the shoulder to dismiss the idea. “Of course not,” she says. “I’m not that type of girl.”
Nearby, Americans in their sixties and seventies drunkenly solicit girls who barely look of age. As I order an Uber, I think of the men seeking sex on the streets of Medellín, and through the apps, who might not survive with their memory intact. I also wonder what sort of poverty, trauma, or outright intimidation might lead these women — Gutiérrez has warned that some of the women in Lleras park have been trafficked — to risk killing a man for his wallet.
Sex workers aren’t the only ones who are allegedly taking advantage of men by using these drugs James Doolin, a Texas businessman, 55, with slicked-back gray hair and bronze skin, met a woman on a dating app believing she wanted to date him.
Doolin welcomes me into his upscale Airbnb on the fifth floor of an apartment block a five-minute walk from Lleras Park. He says he met his ex-wife, who is 18 years younger than him, in Venezuela in 2015. But they divorced six years later, and now he is looking for a new partner. “Attractive women seem to be concentrated here, especially if you prefer Latinas, which I do,” says Doolin.
On Feb. 18, 2025, he said, he went for dinner with a stunning, dark-haired Colombian, who told him her name was Licet and she was 25 after they matched on Bumble. When they went back to his Airbnb with a bottle of champagne, he took precautions. “Just to be safe, I put my phone and my wallet in the safe, and I hid the key in the laundry room. I thought, ‘OK, if anything happens, she’s not gonna get anything.’”
They made small talk, danced, and kissed, and, he says, she asked to stay the night. “I said, ‘Yeah, that’s OK.’ And she excused herself to the bathroom.” When she came back out, she was in her bra. “She took my head, brought it to her chest, and I was out like that,” he recalls. “I believe she applied the drug in powder form to her chest.”
The next morning, he was rushed to hospital.“I guess she said, ‘Hey, go get the key’ and I went and got it, because when I came back to my senses the contents of the safe were missing,” he says. “The thing about that drug is you will do pretty much whatever they say.” His wallet and $1,500 had disappeared along with his phone and laptop. His knee was also badly cut after he fell on a glass shower door.
Doctors did not run a toxicology test, but Doolin believes it was scopolamine. It took him four days to start feeling like himself again, and despite a series of surgeries and experimental treatments, more than a year later, he still walks with a limp. “I’m probably going to need a partial knee replacement,” he says, showing me how the muscle in his left leg has wasted away without exercise. “In my mind, it was pretty much attempted murder.” Days after the incident, he reported her to the police. “Drugging me, that’s crossing another level. She left me there to die.”
Bart Mensink, a roofer from the Netherlands who visited Colombia in October 2025, says he lost far more money than Doolin — though he can still easily walk. Blue-eyed with a dark, coiffed beard, the 29-year-old travel blogger logged onto Tinder when he got to Medellín, and started asking his matches if they would like to make content with him for his YouTube channel. A supposedly 23-year-old woman named Caroli proposed various places to shoot footage, including a salsa class and a traditional restaurant, and so he went to meet her in Laureles, a neighborhood voted the coolest in the world by Time Out magazine in 2023.
“We talked about the plan for the night, and then after a while, she said, ‘Why don’t we order some food at your apartment?’” he says. At his Airbnb, located in a building with in-house security, he poured Bacardi and Cokes. “I take my glass, I take a sip, and from that moment, everything is gone,” he recalls. “I immediately knew when I drank it, I knew I got fucked.” A split second before he lost his memory, Mensink remembers looking at Caroli quizzically, “Like, what’s in the drink? That’s the last memory I have.”
The next thing Mensink remembers, it was two days later and all of his valuables were gone, including expensive camera gear and a drone. “I woke up, and I was like, ‘What the fuck happened?’” he says. “I felt like an old grandpa who lost his memory. I lost all my money, but I also lost the ability to think, the ability to speak.… If I had a drop more, I would have been dead for sure.” He stumbled out of his apartment and sought help from the police, but says they did not take him seriously. “The cops just think, ‘Oh, this is a sex tourist.’”
Mensink connected with his brother and was soon on a flight to meet him on the nearby island of Curaçao. There, according to the story he tells, he discovered his Binance cryptocurrency account, which had held around $116,000 in bitcoins, was empty. The only logical explanation was that he willingly provided the passcodes.
“I was devastated,” Mensink says. He felt like “an idiot,” and feared he would feel the same “for the rest of my life.” In a YouTube video five days after the incident, he was despondent. “The plan, now, is not to commit suicide,” he says in it. “Right now, I just really don’t know what to do with my life.” He never went to the hospital, but made another Tinder account on his new phone and swiped before his flight back to the Netherlands without finding her, until he fell asleep. “And then I woke up and the first swipe was her.” He posted photos of her profile on his YouTube and reported her to the police.
“It was like going from living the good life to a total dark place of depression,” he says. “I lost all my money.” He has since created a number of other videos about the episode on his monetized channel.
San Francisco native Steve Hamilton runs the YouTube channel Medellín Unfiltered. Though he’s never been drugged with scopolamine, he was sedated with benzodiazepines and robbed several years ago, and has devoted much of his channel to warning tourists about the risks. As I set about to discover whether I could find the drug, he tells me that scopolamine can be procured in an area in the center of Medellín known as the Bronx. “There’s an open-air drug market,” he says. “I never feel intimidated going places, but I’ve been there, and it’s the scariest place I’ve been to in South America — and I’ve been to Venezuela. It’s very dangerous.”
I ask a local taxi to go on a drive-through of the Bronx, past invisible lines the Uber drivers would not broach, and he agrees for the relatively high price of $4. The Bronx spans several blocks of Calle 56 and looks like a junkyard apocalypse. Trash is strewn everywhere; people addicted to the cheap stimulant basuco, derived from cocaine-production residue, lumber around in varying states of distress. As we drive through, every eyeball in the vicinity is fixed on our little yellow taxi, and I hastily roll up my window. I chat with the driver about the criminals who run the block. “They can drug you and rob you and put you in acid and disappear you,” he says.
Two drug dealers who appear to be in their forties approach our vehicle. I enquire whether scopolamine could be purchased in the Bronx. “Si, pero es muy delicado (Yes, but it’s a sensitive issue),” one of the men replies. “For scopolamine, it’s 12 years in jail,” he adds. To that end, he offers me a gram — enough to kill several people — for $30, but I would have to give him the money in cash and wait 15 minutes for his return with the goods.
Our taxi driver, nonchalantly smoking a joint, did not think this a wise idea. He believed we could be ambushed, attacked, and robbed. I duly requested that we get out of there — after all, I did not want any scopolamine, really — and the driver asked for an extra $4 for his trouble. I quickly handed it over.
NEAR THE BRONX, IN A MODEST apartment above a convenience store, a sex worker named Maria showed the drug on camera as part of a 2024 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4. Sitting on her bed in a sparsely furnished room, Maria’s face was blurred to protect her identity. She wore a white zip-front crop top beneath a black Adidas jacket, as well as surgical gloves. She admitted to drugging men with scopolamine and gave the presenter a mask so he did not accidentally inhale the substance. “If I get the measurements wrong, it will just kill them,” she said casually of her victims.
Maria claimed she’s worked for one of Medellín’s criminal gangs from age eight, as she showed the camera small white rocks of scopolamine, similar to crack cocaine. “With this single rock, I can put more than three or four people to sleep,” she said, wearing a mask, explaining she would make 100 times more money drugging and robbing than simply selling sex. Given that she works for a gang, however, she will never see much of the profit. Maria put a thimble-size piece of scopolamine into a liquid spray bottle and it quickly dissolved. “One spray and they’re out cold,” she told the interviewer. Asked if she ever killed anyone, she replied: “I hope not, but certainly it’s possible.”
Police reports from foreign men who claim they have been “scopolamined” have been increasing, according to Capt. Andrés Arboleda, head of theft for Medellín’s police. There were 443 cases last year, but in the first five months of 2026, there were 304 reports — suggesting the yearly number was set to spike. This increase was seemingly due to the rise in tourism and the targeting of foreign men by criminal groups. “Some ended up in hospitals, others collapsed in Airbnbs, others in hotels,” Arboleda says.
But the police also caution that many stories involving scopolamine verge on urban legend, and confirm that most criminals use other sedative drugs to manipulate their victims. “It’s very difficult to manufacture and administer,” Arboleda says. “If you exceed the proper dose, the person can be left like a baby, or die.” The aftereffects can be permanent, he warns. “I’ve known people who have been left in diapers.”
At Medellín City Hall, a hulking complex of concrete towers, where police and municipal officials work side by side, I meet with Medellín’s secretary of security, Manuel Villa, a lawyer by trade who is allied with the mayor’s center-right political movement. In June last year, a group of three women, Las Mamacitas, were arrested after allegedly drugging men they had met on dating apps and through social media with scopolamine, but it is unclear whether police were able to confirm the use of the drug. “We continue to dismantle criminal networks that use cowardly methods such as scopolamine,” Villa said in a press release at the time.
“We are going after those who try to use seduction to camouflage their crime. We will not allow groups like this to continue operating with impunity,” he said.
In March 2025, police arrested five women who initially were alleged to have used scopolamine to steal more than 600,000,000 pesos — about $160,000 — from 23 foreigners from countries including the U.S., Australia, Germany, and Norway. Authorities started calling the group Las Barbies, who they said primarily operated out of Lleras Park, but it later emerged that the group used the drug Clonazepam, a benzodiazepine, to drug their victims. The case has yet to reach trial. “It’s been going on for a long time,” Villa tells me of the issue. “We’ve chosen to make it visible so we can confront it.”
Though grateful he survived, Doolin remains frustrated that the police still have not caught his attacker. He put up posters around Lleras Park offering a $5,000 reward for information alongside photos of Licet with red lipstick and thick eyebrows. Doolin soon discovered her real name, actual age — which was a few years younger than she had claimed — and parents’ address, which he passed to police at the end of last year, but he is still awaiting further action. “I hope the police find her before I do,” he says.
Mensink, meanwhile, is traveling through Europe and North Africa with nearly no money — unwilling to give up his dream of being a travel vlogger. In a recent Instagram post on what he now calls his “Travel No Money” journey, he was seen accepting a free ride from a 12-year-old Moroccan child. “The money is gone, but I’m still alive,” he tells me.
In late March, however, an American man died after a night out in Medellín. Eric Fernando Gutiérrez Molina, 32, was a flight attendant passing through the city. Molina went out with a co-worker, but they became separated and the co-worker later returned to their hotel “somewhat disoriented,” Villa told reporters. Molina was found dead days later, some 50 miles south of where they were staying. Villa says it’s clear Molina encountered people “with a history of committing theft” with scopolamine.
The number of foreign men who have been killed in suspicious or downright violent circumstances in Medellín in recent years continues to grow. According to reports, Jean Roody Dagobert, a 36-year-old American, died in late June after spending the night with women he and his friends met in Lleras Park. A video appears to show one of the women exiting from the man’s apartment by jumping from a second-floor window.
But many visitors, like Mark, don’t report the criminals who drug and almost kill them. Toxicologist Fernández has stayed in touch with his patient and still winces about how Mark feared reporting the crime to the police could reflect poorly on him professionally. He says Mark is still coping with long-term effects. “He suffered major memory impairment, as well as difficulty concentrating and making decisions,” says Fernández. “It almost cost him his life.”
Contributors: Edinson Arroyo
results.summary:
Foreign tourists in Medellín, Colombia, are increasingly targeted by criminal gangs using scopolamine and other sedatives to induce compliance, leading to widespread robberies, hospitalizations, and unexplained deaths.

### Key Points
- Scopolamine, derived from the brugmansia flower, is a tasteless, odorless substance that can induce a zombie-like state of total compliance.
- Criminals often use dating apps or target visitors in nightlife hubs like Lleras Park to lure victims into private settings before administering drugs.
- While often referred to as "scopolamine," many perpetrators now use benzodiazepines like Clonazepam, which are easier to obtain and manage.
- Medellín police reported 443 drugging cases last year, with 304 reports filed in the first five months of 2026 alone.
- Victims frequently suffer from severe memory loss, organ failure, and significant financial theft, with some incidents resulting in fatalities.

### Why it Matters
The surge in drugging incidents highlights the growing risks associated with Medellín’s booming sex tourism industry and the vulnerability of foreign visitors. These crimes pose a significant challenge to local authorities attempting to balance the city's reputation as a global travel destination with the need to dismantle organized criminal networks.

results.title: Democrats Are Failing the Waymo Test
results.author: Rogé Karma
results.content:
Sign up for Work in Progress, a newsletter where Rogé Karma investigates the mysteries of a complicated economy.
The driverless future is here—but, to borrow from William Gibson, it’s not evenly distributed. Waymo’s self-driving robotaxis are available in cities in California, Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Tennessee, and Texas. Aside from California, where the technology originated, those are all red or purple states. In every other blue state, meanwhile, driverless taxis are still not allowed to operate. If you live in Miami or Dallas, you can summon a Waymo to get where you’re going. If you live in Boston or New York, you can’t.
This is not an accident. In Democratic jurisdictions, a coalition of labor unions, anti-tech activists, and politicians have kept driverless vehicles off the streets. (Colorado, which passed a bill authorizing driverless vehicles in 2017, before the current backlash, is on track to become the exception later this year.) They argue that the new technology would make the roads more dangerous and throw millions of human drivers out of work, all to enrich a handful of tech oligarchs.
A version of this fight is now playing out in Washington, D.C., where Kamala Harris won more than 90 percent of the vote in 2024 and where local officials recently introduced a bill that would provide a pathway for robotaxis to begin operating. Some residents have welcomed that prospect. But others are digging in their heels. Bill Davis, the president of the local Teamsters union, declared in a statement that the legislation “doesn’t benefit anyone outside of Silicon Valley billionaires” and “comes at the expense of middle-class professional drivers and anyone else who wants safer streets in our city.”
Driverless cars will indeed cost some workers their jobs. But unlike so many other recent Silicon Valley innovations, they have already demonstrated the potential to bring immense societal benefits. About 40,000 Americans die in car accidents every year. The number of crash-related injuries is much larger. As many as 10,000 crash victims enter emergency rooms around the country every day. Waymos are so much safer than human drivers that deploying them widely could avert countless injuries and deaths every year.
They will also make transportation more affordable: A taxi without a driver is much cheaper. Waymo is currently more expensive than Uber and Lyft, but that’s largely because supply is artificially constrained and demand is high. The price differential is dropping fast and will go away soon. Waymos also show promise in reducing carbon emissions and air pollution (the cars are electric), and providing reliable access to people who live in poor neighborhoods (who are routinely turned down by rideshare drivers). Saying no to Waymo is saying no to a technology that will change the world for the better.
There is a name for a political movement that taps into people’s resistance to change and defense of the status quo. William F. Buckley famously described a conservative as “someone who stands athwart history, yelling Stop.” Progressivism was founded on the opposite ethic: that scientific and technological progress can bring about a better, more equitable future, provided that it’s steered in the right direction. In this sense, self-driving cars are a test for American progressives—a test of whether they have become so captured by interest groups, so hostile to corporations, and so fearful of technological change that they’ve transformed into enemies of progress itself.
In much of the country, the popular conception of self-driving cars is something between a bumbling idiot and a mechanical death trap. Videos of Waymo vehicles making ridiculous errors go viral online. Earlier this year, a Waymo hit a child who ran into the road near an elementary school in Santa Monica, California, causing minor injuries. When a jurisdiction considers whether to allow Waymos, stories like these come up again and again. “I’m also deeply concerned about the safety issues autonomous vehicles have already had in other cities,” Helen Raynor-Hughes, a longtime D.C.-area resident, testified during a public hearing in July, citing “reports of crashes, traffic disruptions, and situations where these vehicles failed to respond properly to pedestrians, cyclists, and other drivers.”
But anecdotes can mislead. The question is how robotaxis’ error rate stacks up against that of human drivers. In a recent study, researchers at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety compared the crash and accident data on a per-mile basis for Waymo vehicles with those of human drivers in the cities where Waymos operated from 2021 to 2024. They found that Waymos were involved in 68 percent fewer crashes serious enough to be reported to police and 81 percent fewer crashes that caused an injury. These findings are “likely conservative” because human drivers regularly fail to report accidents, Eric Teoh, the report’s lead author, told me.
Several other studies have produced even more favorable results. These studies are co-authored by Waymo researchers but have been peer-reviewed by independent academics. Every expert I spoke with for this story, including Waymo skeptics, told me that they consider the research to be high-quality. “Reductions this big are basically unheard of when it comes to traffic safety,” Noah Goodall, a senior research scientist at the Virginia Transportation Research Council, told me. “Not even seat belts or airbags achieved the kinds of numbers we’re seeing here.” (Waymo, which is owned by Alphabet, is the only company that has demonstrated such a strong safety record. The others, including Tesla, have not disclosed the data needed to make safety claims.)
Even these figures probably underestimate how safe Waymos are. The journalists Timothy B. Lee and Kai Williams recently reviewed the details of the 78 accidents that Waymo vehicles had been involved in over a seven-month period and that were serious enough to cause an injury or trigger an airbag deployment. They found just one example where Waymo “could plausibly bear some responsibility” for a taxi crashing into another vehicle or a pedestrian—the Santa Monica–school incident—and another three where culpability was “mixed or unclear.” “We went into this looking for any evidence that Waymo could even remotely be at fault for a given crash,” Lee told me. “But those cases were just really hard to find.”
The big caveat to Waymo’s safety record is its difficulty with so-called edge cases—unpredictable situations for which its algorithm is unprepared and in which human judgment really comes in handy. When a power outage knocked out a third of San Francisco’s traffic lights last December, at least 60 Waymos abruptly idled mid-road, causing severe gridlock and delays. Something similar happened to a few dozen Waymos this year when the driverless vehicles encountered unexpected road closures during San Francisco’s Fourth of July celebrations. Waymos have obstructed emergency vehicles in several cities, typically because of their tendency to freeze when they encounter alarms, sirens, or temporary road closures. The company has not done nearly enough to fix the problem. “Competent driving is about a lot more than crash statistics,” Philip Koopman, an emeritus professor of engineering at Carnegie Mellon, told me. “If Waymo isn’t able to address some of these problematic patterns, it is going to be very hard to convince the public they are safe.”
Even so, the fact that Waymos are considerably safer than human drivers is undeniable. A robot driver can’t drink and drive, fall asleep at the wheel, or check its phone. It won’t flout the rules of the road when it’s running late or trying to impress its friends. And it is equipped with more than a dozen different cameras, plus radar and laser sensors, meaning it doesn’t have blind spots. Bryant Walker Smith, an associate law professor at the University of South Carolina, has advised governments on how to regulate self-driving cars. “What I always tell policy makers is that we absolutely should be concerned about automated driving,” he told me. “But we should be terrified of human driving.”
Safety might be the average American’s top concern about driverless cars, but the average American isn’t spearheading the political resistance to Waymo. Labor unions are. The campaign against driverless vehicles has been led by a coalition of unions representing taxi, rideshare, and truck drivers who argue that self-driving cars will destroy millions of working-class jobs. (Although experts believe that self-driving trucks and delivery vehicles are at least several years away from being a regular presence on roads, labor unions see robotaxi legalization as a stepping stone to a fully automated driving future.) Indeed, Helen Raynor-Hughes, the area resident who testified about Waymo’s safety record, began by identifying herself as a Service Employees International Union member who drives for Uber and Lyft.
In 2026 alone, this Labor United Against Waymo coalition has helped defeat or delay legislation to authorize driverless vehicles in Illinois, Minnesota, Maryland, Virginia, Oregon, and Washington State. In January, New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared that she would pursue a bill to allow robotaxis to operate in the state, only to backtrack a few weeks later following an outcry from labor leaders.
When I arrived at D.C.’s city hall in July for a public hearing on the proposed bill to authorize Waymo, I passed dozens of protesters from various labor groups chanting and holding signs with slogans such as WAYMO? HELL NO and AI DOESN’T VOTE. We Do. Inside, about a dozen labor leaders and rideshare drivers demanded that city officials vote against the bill. Crystal Middleton, a D.C. resident who drives Uber and Lyft part-time to support her family, testified that if Waymo were adopted in the city, “many D.C. families, including mine, will struggle to make ends meet.”
I’m sympathetic to that argument. When I was growing up, my dad spent years driving Uber and Lyft on the weekends to help pay the bills. Like many drivers, he resented the meager pay and lack of benefits. (There’s an irony that unions and Democratic lawmakers are rallying to defend the type of precarious gig work that they have spent more than a decade criticizing.) But it’s hard to imagine what our family would have done without the extra income. The impulse to protect workers like him—not to mention the delivery and truck drivers who fear that they’ll be next—from being displaced by a new technology is understandable.
That approach, however, ignores the larger number of people who would benefit from a change to the status quo. At the public hearing, local nonprofit leaders and politicians, including Shane Simenstad, the director of public policy for Safe Kids Worldwide, pointed out that rideshare drivers often refuse to enter less desirable parts of the city, leaving residents of poor neighborhoods without a reliable way to get to work or school. Claire Stanley, the director of advocacy and governmental affairs for the American Council of the Blind, spoke about being denied Uber and Lyft rides because of her service dog. Multiple women testified about their fear of being harassed or assaulted by rideshare drivers. (According to a 2025 New York Times investigation, Uber received a report of sexual assault or misconduct nearly every eight minutes on average in the U.S. from 2017 to 2022.)
Some of the most moving testimonies came from the victims of car crashes and their loved ones. Rameez Tase, a local resident and avid cyclist, told the story of a friend who had been nearly killed after being hit by a car. “Anyone who knows me well knows that my biggest fear of death is being struck and killed by a distracted driver—and leaving my three young children without a father for the rest of their lives,” he said. Cesar Toledo, a member of the D.C. Commission on Poverty, recounted a childhood “marked by the terrifying reality of riding in vehicles driven by family members under the influence.”
Car accidents kill roughly as many Americans each year as breast cancer does, and twice the number of people who die from homicides. It is a leading cause of death among children and young adults. “The number of traffic deaths in America is the equivalent of a Boeing 737 crashing every single day,” Jonathan Slotkin, a neurosurgeon who regularly treats crash victims, told me. “That’s what we’ve chosen to tolerate as the price of mobility.”
Waymos, to be clear, wouldn’t solve this problem right away. Although rideshare and taxi drivers get into accidents at higher rates than the average driver, they make up a small fraction of cars on the road. But operating robotaxis is a key step for Waymo and other companies to perfect their self-driving technology, which could then be sold to vehicle manufacturers like Toyota to include as an optional feature in every car. “If we had a drug that showed these kinds of results, we’d be doing everything we could to get it out to as many people as fast as possible,” Slotkin said.
Widespread adoption of driverless vehicles would further a litany of goals that anyone should celebrate, especially those who claim to be progressive: slashing traffic injuries and deaths; helping the poor and disabled secure stable employment; making cities safer places to bike and walk; reducing the prevelance of sexual assault and misconduct; putting more electric vehicles on the roads. And yet progressives are the ones standing in the way. “Honestly, it’s just embarrassing,” Colin Mortimer, the director of the Center for New Liberalism, a center-left advocacy group, told me. “Liberals are always talking about how we’re the party that believes in science, that believes in data, that believes in helping the vulnerable. But on this issue we’re doing the exact opposite.”
Some Washington, D.C., legislators believe that the nation’s capital can pioneer a different approach to Waymo. In May, the D.C. Council member Charles Allen introduced a bill that would authorize driverless vehicles to begin operating in the district, but only if their makers meet certain key conditions designed in part to address the edge-case problem and reduce the impact on the city’s labor force. These include completing stringent testing and safety requirements and submitting a plan for interacting with first responders. Even then, the total number of driverless vehicles would be capped at a few hundred during the initial rollout. Each vehicle would also be subject to a per-mile tax used to fund public transit, as well as workforce training and compensation for displaced rideshare and taxi drivers. “We have to be honest with ourselves: This technology is already here and is only going to become a bigger part of our lives going forward,” Allen told me a few weeks after the hearing. “And so we can either bury our heads in the sand and have this change happen to us. Or we can put guardrails in place to make sure the technology works for us and our communities.”
In Allen’s view, too many restrictions would risk throttling a technology that could otherwise bring huge benefits; too few would invite a high-profile incident that draws a public backlash. Getting the balance right will be difficult. My own view is that the bill should have more restrictive testing requirements around edge cases—for instance, simulating power outages or major emergencies—before driverless vehicles can be deployed. But it should also create a less bureaucratic process for increasing the number of vehicles once those requirements have been met. The bill also faces several political obstacles, including an incoming mayor who expressed skepticism about Waymo expansion on the campaign trail. But Allen is trying to do something that no city has done before: chart a middle course between letting the new technology rip and blocking it altogether.
One-hundred and fifty years ago, the United States was experiencing the advent of a brand-new transportation technology. Railroads reduced cross-country travel from months to days, turned the U.S. into an industrial powerhouse, and enabled the modern consumer economy. But they also displaced workers, such as canal operators and stagecoach drivers; led to skyrocketing inequality; and produced corrupt monopolies presided over by ruthless oligarchs. A new political movement formed in response. Its adherents passed legislation that protected workers, created novel regulatory agencies, broke up powerful monopolies, and developed safety standards. Neither techno-utopians nor luddites, they believed that technology could be a force for progress—but only if it was actively shaped and regulated by the public. They thus called themselves progressives. Their political descendants would do well to remember their example.
results.summary:
Waymo’s expansion of driverless robotaxis faces significant political resistance in Democratic-led cities, sparking a national debate over balancing technological safety benefits against potential labor market disruptions.

### Key Points
- Waymo currently operates autonomous vehicles in California, Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Tennessee, and Texas, while facing legislative blocks in many blue states.
- Research from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety indicates Waymo vehicles are involved in 68% fewer police-reported crashes and 81% fewer injury-related crashes than human drivers.
- Labor unions, including the Teamsters and various rideshare driver groups, are leading the opposition, citing concerns over job displacement and the impact on professional drivers.
- Critics highlight "edge case" failures, such as vehicles idling during power outages or obstructing emergency responders, as significant safety and operational hurdles.
- Washington, D.C. is considering a compromise bill that would authorize robotaxis while implementing per-mile taxes to fund public transit and workforce training for displaced drivers.

### Why it Matters
The debate over autonomous vehicles serves as a critical test for modern progressivism, forcing a choice between protecting the status quo for labor groups and embracing technology that could drastically reduce traffic fatalities. Successfully integrating this technology requires a regulatory middle ground that addresses legitimate safety and economic concerns without stifling innovation that offers clear societal benefits.

results.title: I thought this Motorola app was bloatware — now I can’t live without it
results.author: Zac Kew-Denniss
results.content:
I thought this Motorola app was bloatware — now I can't live without it
Aug 19, 2026 — 5:30 AM ET
I uninstall a lot of the pre-loaded apps and software that come with some phones and computers. Many of them are nothing more than bloat I’ll never use. If you have a Motorola phone, you might assume this is true of the Smart Connect app.
Smart Connect comes preloaded on Motorola phones and Lenovo laptops, but it can be used on any Android or Windows device. I decided to give it a shot on my Motorola Razr before uninstalling it, and I couldn’t be happier that I did.
If you haven’t tried Smart Connect yet, take this as your sign to change that.
Which Smart Connect feature would you use the most?
Easy file sharing
I do a lot of file sharing between my PC and phones. Quick Share and Blip are good, but Smart Connect has an advantage over both. To get an image from my phone, I don’t need to unlock it and send the file. Smart Connect lets me browse the images from my computer and pull them over. The exception to this rule is iOS devices — you can use Smart Connect for file sharing on the iPhone and iPad, but you have to send them from the device.
Microsoft’s Link to Windows includes this and many of the features we’ll look at here, but it’s a chore if you’re using more than one phone or tablet. You have to select and connect to a different device each time, whereas Smart Connect stays connected to all your devices at once.
Wireless webcam, even for a Pixel
It’s been a while since Google updated Pixel phones so they could be used as a webcam on your PC. It only works when your Pixel is connected via a cable, though. Smart Connect lets any Android phone serve as a wireless webcam, which I find much more convenient.
I know that plugging your phone into your PC isn’t the end of the world, but my computer is quite a distance from where I sit at my desk, and having to route a cable (or remember where I have a cable long enough) on the few occasions I make video calls is a faff that’s easily avoided with Smart Connect.
App streaming for Motorola phones
Screen sharing is more advanced than you’d think with Smart Connect, and my only criticism is that it only works with Motorola phones. As you can see in the images above, you can mirror your phone screen or start a virtual display. The first of these is exactly what you’re thinking — whatever content is on your phone screen gets mirrored to the PC. It’s the virtual phone option that I use the most.
When I’m working, I often have my phone on my desk playing a YouTube playlist as background noise. I’ve never bothered using screen mirroring to open the app and mark off what I need to because doing so would mean using my keyboard and trackpad to try and exit YouTube and go to the app I want.
Streaming a single app from the Smart Connect main screen is one solution, but if I want to get multiple things done on my phone without my video pausing, virtual phone mode does that. It creates a separate desktop environment on your PC that doesn’t stop whatever is happening on the phone’s screen. Something else I especially appreciate is that the virtual phone adds home, back, recent, and other buttons to the bottom of the window, so you don’t have to use your trackpad to simulate touch inputs for those actions.
If you want to take things further, you can use Smart Connect’s desktop mode. It’s Motorola’s version of Samsung DeX, and as far as these mobile desktop experiences go, it’s pretty good. Usually, you’d have to plug the phone into a monitor with an HDMI cable, but Smart Connect on a PC lets you do it wirelessly. This isn’t something I use much. If I’m already on a PC and I can use Smart Connect to access all of the files on my phone anyway, I’d rather do that than run a virtual desktop. If this is something you use on the regular, though, having wireless access is a good thing.
Easy casting to TV
In the Smart Connect app on a Motorola phone, there’s a menu for connected displays. Here you’ll find anything that supports Miracast or Google Cast. Google Cast displays will just mirror the display or a single app, just like a Pixel. But Miracast devices, like my old Roku, get a suite of features that Motorola has added that are really fun. Your phone can simulate plenty of input methods, from a trackpad to a virtual mouse that you point at the TV, although I found it less than usable and stuck to the keypad or trackpad.
You can launch the previously mentioned Desktop Mode and mirror your display, but what stood out to me are the TV and game hubs. These let you cast any game or media app to your TV while keeping the phone as the controller. Admittedly, I couldn’t test this out as much as I’d like. My Roku is truly ancient, and my Razr had to use a compatibility mode just to connect to it.
Screen mirroring was fine, but casting media was like watching a slideshow. With a newer Roku that didn’t have that problem, I could see myself using this. In this case, the phone streams the game to the TV, and you use a Bluetooth controller to play. I love the idea of cozying up in bed and playing Stardew Valley on the TV without having to move my PS5 from the other room.
If you aren’t using Smart Connect, you should
If you’ve got a Motorola phone, then using Smart Connect is a no-brainer. It’s preinstalled and has features that will be useful to many people. If you don’t have a Moto but use multiple Android devices and a Windows PC, it’s still worth checking out, especially if your Android gadgets come from multiple brands. Usually, apps and services like this lock everything into an ecosystem, but file transfers, clipboard sync, and wireless webcams work on anything.
Simply put, there are many reasons to try Smart Connect. Whether you already have it on a Motorola phone or want to download it on another Android phone, I can’t recommend it enough.
results.summary:
Motorola’s pre-installed Smart Connect app offers versatile cross-device functionality, enabling seamless file sharing, wireless webcam usage, and app streaming between Android smartphones and Windows-based personal computers.

### Key Points
- Smart Connect allows users to browse and transfer files from a phone to a PC without needing to unlock the mobile device.
- The software enables any Android phone to function as a wireless webcam for PC video calls, bypassing the need for physical cables.
- Users can mirror their phone screens or launch a virtual desktop environment on a PC to manage multiple mobile apps simultaneously.
- The app supports wireless casting to Miracast and Google Cast displays, including specialized hubs for gaming and media playback.
- While some advanced features are exclusive to Motorola hardware, core utilities like file transfers and clipboard syncing work across most Android devices.

### Why it Matters
This software challenges the restrictive nature of proprietary ecosystems by offering a flexible, multi-device connectivity suite that works across various Android brands and Windows PCs. By simplifying complex tasks like wireless screen mirroring and file management, it provides a practical alternative to more limited tools like Microsoft’s Link to Windows.

results.title: Striking hospital employees sound alarm over workplace violence
results.author: Lynn Arditi
results.content:
Striking hospital employees sound alarm over workplace violence
Nurse Crystal Dhooghe is used to dealing with blood and broken bones in the emergency room. But she didn't expect to witness so much violence against her own colleagues.
"I've seen nurses get shoved, pushed, scratched. The biggest one is bitten," said Dhooghe, who works at Henry Ford Genesys Hospital in Grand Blanc, Mich.
The prevalence of workplace violence in healthcare has fueled strikes in states such as Louisiana, New York, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island and Michigan, where Dhooghe and many of her co-workers have been on the picket line since Labor Day of last year.
"People will question me and be like, 'Why are you still working in a place if you're treated like this?'" said Dhooghe, who gets by on strike benefits and working extra shifts at another hospital. The problem, she said, is that other hospitals aren't any better. "It's the same everywhere I go."
In a statement, Henry Ford spokesperson Dana Jay acknowledged violence against healthcare workers is a "national epidemic" and said the health system's efforts to address the problem include metal detectors, armed security officers trained to make "misdemeanor arrests" and de-escalation training.
"We have zero tolerance for violence of any kind," said Jay, asserting the strike is not about safety but is instead "simply an economic strike."
Nationwide, hospital workers are seven times as likely to be injured on the job due to violent acts as members of the general working population, according to the most recent data available from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The outcry over workplace violence in healthcare is pitting workers' demands for better compensation and staffing against hospital operators pressured to cut costs.
When ERs feel like "a powder keg"
Violent outbursts are so common that they've been dramatized on the popular medical TV series The Pitt.
"Emergency rooms right now are like a powder keg," said Rachel Odes, an assistant professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison School of Nursing.
In hospitals, a combative or violent patient is known as a "code gray." Outbursts can be spontaneous and unpredictable, making some almost impossible to prevent.
But research shows the risk of violence increases when hospitals are understaffed or employees are insufficiently trained or experienced.
Mental health worker Andrew Kimball-Mirzaie said he got hurt in February 2024 at Butler Hospital in Providence, R.I.
He'd been working at the private psychiatric hospital for about six weeks and said he hadn't yet worked in the ER.
He said he was sent there to "monitor" a man in his 20s who was waiting for an inpatient bed.
The patient was alone in a back room watching a Knicks basketball game on TV, he recalled. Kimball-Mirzaie said he got the patient a drink and a snack.
They were watching the game when, suddenly, he said, the patient stood up and punched him in the face.
He said the assault left him with a concussion and broken nose. His injuries were documented in the hospital's incident log.
"I understand that there is an inherent danger with the job," Kimball-Mirzaie said.
He doesn't blame the patient, who was very ill at the time. "We should have had at least another staff member with us," he said, "and I should have been adequately trained on the unit."
The attack emboldened Kimball-Mirzaie to join some 700 other unionized Butler workers last spring and summer in a months-long strike, which forced the hospital to close nearly half of its beds.
Service Employees International Union 1199 New England declared the strike a win.
Employees received wage increases that union leaders said would enable the hospital to attract and retain more staff.
The hospital also agreed to provide financial support for workers violently injured on the job. And the hospital and union agreed to jointly fund a "time bank" to supplement workers' compensation for injured workers who need more time to recover.
But five months later, a nurse supervisor at Butler had to call 911 because an unarmed patient in the hospital's ER was assaulting staff. According to the police report, by the time police arrested the patient, he'd injured two nurses, a security guard and a police officer.
"Butler recognizes the importance of being proactive in protecting those who provide care," Mary Marran, Butler's president and chief operating officer, said in a statement. She added that hospital leadership meets regularly with staff to review safety measures and "identify opportunities to strengthen protection for everyone."
The patient was charged with four counts of felony assault, including against the two nurses.
The American Hospital Association has said punishment is key to preventing violence. It has been lobbying Congress to make assaulting healthcare workers a federal crime that would carry up to 10 years in prison.
At least 45 states, including Michigan and Rhode Island, have enacted similar laws.
But workplace safety experts say there is no evidence that such laws have reduced the incidence of violence against healthcare workers.
Calls for "safe staffing"
Striking healthcare workers around the country often have demanded "safe staffing" instead of stronger punishments for patients who cause injuries.
The rise in violence against healthcare workers has caught the attention of the Joint Commission, the accreditation organization for more than 80% of U.S. hospitals and health systems.
The commission released national performance goals that took effect in January and require hospitals to be properly staffed and that staff be trained "to provide safe, quality care."
But no federal law limits the number of patients in a nurse's care across healthcare settings. The nation's largest nurses union, National Nurses United, having pressed for a national standard since 2018.
Hospitals must "safely staff all units" to enable nurses to "provide the care that patients need before they get agitated or disoriented," said Jane Thomason, lead industrial hygienist for National Nurses United.
Some states have passed their own staffing laws. Only California has enacted broad mandatory nurse staffing ratios, which research shows were associated with lower mortality rates and likely higher retention. Oregon enacted a staffing law, with exceptions.
Legislators in Massachusetts and New Jersey have introduced similar bills, but they have failed to advance to floor votes.
The American Hospital Association opposes mandatory minimum nurse staffing ratios in hospitals, saying they would "remove real-time clinical judgment and flexibility," compound staffing shortages, and potentially force some hospitals to turn away patients or delay care, spokesperson Colleen Kincaid said.
Kincaid also pointed to California, whose new emergency nurse staffing ratios for psychiatric hospitals reportedly forced bed closures in at least four counties.
"There are a lot of other things you can do to prevent workplace violence than just increasing staffing levels," said Jordan Barab, who was a deputy assistant secretary of labor for the Occupational Safety and Health Administration during the Obama administration and helped develop OSHA's 2016 guidelines for healthcare and social service workers.
Barab said hospitals can, for example, train employees in de-escalation, install metal detectors, or have specially trained security guards on-site so staff members don't have to wait for police to arrive when an incident happens.
The health provisions in President Trump's signature tax-and-spending law will squeeze hospitals' finances in the next few years, said Debbie Berkowitz, a worker safety and health policy expert at Georgetown University.
When funding dries up, she said, "protecting workers is going to be the first thing that gets cut."

Healthcare workers across the United States are increasingly organizing strikes to demand safer staffing levels and better protections against rising rates of workplace violence in hospital settings.

### Key Points
- Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows hospital employees are seven times more likely to suffer work-related injuries from violence than the general workforce.
- Striking workers at facilities like Henry Ford Genesys Hospital and Butler Hospital cite understaffing and insufficient training as primary drivers of violent incidents.
- The Joint Commission implemented new national performance goals in January 2024 requiring hospitals to maintain proper staffing and provide safety training.
- While the American Hospital Association advocates for federal criminal penalties for assaulting staff, unions like National Nurses United prioritize mandatory staffing ratios.
- Only California currently enforces broad mandatory nurse staffing ratios, though similar legislation has been introduced but stalled in states like Massachusetts and New Jersey.

### Why it Matters
The ongoing conflict between hospital operators and labor unions highlights a critical tension between cost-cutting measures and the need for secure clinical environments. As financial pressures on healthcare systems grow, the debate over whether to prioritize punitive legal measures or structural staffing mandates will continue to shape national labor relations and patient care standards.

results.title: Rethinking secure file transfer for a cross-domain world
results.author: James Neilson
results.content:
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre recently issued a blunt warning to government and industry alike, warning that many systems are now connected "in ways their designers never anticipated", built on protocols never intended to withstand the sophistication of today's attackers.
That warning applies to all organizations relying on cross-domain processes to move data between environments with different security levels, and especially to complex cyber-physical systems where data flows between standard IT and operational technology (OT) assets.
File transfer is one of these fundamental processes but remains one of the most often overlooked.
SVP International at OPSWAT.
Every invoice sent to a supplier, every firmware update pushed to a factory floor, every report shared with a regulator is data crossing between systems with different levels of trust.
For years, file transfer security has been treated as a solved problem. Enterprises were happy to encrypt the channel, confirm delivery, and move on. That approach made sense when systems were simpler, and threats moved more slowly. However, it no longer reflects reality.
Why perimeter-based trust no longer holds
Most file transfer platforms were never built with security as the primary goal. They were built to move data reliably between systems, encrypt the connection, confirm that a file arrived, and log that the job was done. Whether the file itself was safe was rarely part of the equation.
That gap provides a consistent way for cyber attackers to gain a foothold in their targets' systems. A file transfer platform sits between organizations by design, trusted by both sides precisely because it's meant to be routine infrastructure.

The traditional Managed File Transfer (MFT) model is built to automate file delivery, not to defend against attack. As such, it leaves the process exposed to a familiar set of threats, from man-in-the-middle interception and credential theft to malware covertly embedded in an otherwise ordinary file. Attackers don't need to break the platform itself, only to exploit the assumption that whatever moves through it can be trusted.
As we've seen with incidents like 2023's MoveIT supply chain cyberattack and last year's SharePoint breach, a single vulnerability in a widely used transfer tool can give attackers access to thousands of organizations at once, simply because every one of them assumed the platform itself could be trusted.
That assumption is exactly what attackers are counting on. Securing the channel a file travels through was never the same as securing the file.
The shrinking window to respond
File security has always been a blind spot, but it's become much more critical in recent years as the attack lifecycle continues to accelerate. Newly disclosed vulnerabilities are now routinely exploited within 48 hours of becoming public, leaving little room for patch management by organizations to prepare, or even notice before they're targeted.
Detection, by contrast, still moves comparatively slowly. Breaches involving file-based attacks can go unnoticed for months, giving an intruder ample time to move laterally, extract data, or embed themselves further into connected systems before anyone realizes something is wrong.
It's not simply that attackers are fast, but that most organizations still treat file movement as something to review after the fact rather than control at the point of entry. By the time a malicious file is identified, the damage has often already been done.
This is why proactive, layered controls around every file entering or leaving the business matter more than ever. Waiting to react is not a viable strategy.
Establishing continuous file verification
Closing this gap means shifting towards a security-first MFT process, where every file, user, and workflow is treated as a potential point of exposure rather than assumed safe by default.
Prevention is by design, rather than protection bolted on afterwards as with most traditional MFT models. And that starts with looking inside the file, not just authenticating the channel it arrives through.
Deep content inspection examines the file's actual structure, identifying hidden or malicious elements that a simple scan would miss. Alongside this, automated vulnerability detection and malware prevention should apply to every file by default, not as an optional extra reserved for high-risk transfers. Even the most innocuous file can now serve as a powerful attack vector – in fact, threat actors are counting on it.
Likewise, savvier attackers are actively designing payloads to evade detection, so standard processes need backup. Potentially malicious files need to be tested in a safe, isolated environment where their behavior can be observed before they ever reach a live system. This kind of sandboxing catches clues missed by reputation checks and static scanning, revealing intent rather than simply checking for known signatures.
A Content Disarm and Reconstruction (CDR) process is a valuable addition here, deconstructing files and sanitizing them by removing any active content without harming function.
However, none of this works as a single checkpoint. Each of these controls needs to feed into a continuous process, where a file is validated at every stage of its journey rather than cleared once and trusted from that point on. These capabilities should also be paired with constant monitoring and detailed audit visibility, so that if something does slip through, organizations know exactly what moved, where it went, and what it touched.
As a result, organizations can reliably build confidence in data as it crosses between environments, rather than assuming that confidence once and carrying it forward unchecked.
Closing the loop on trust
The NCSC's warning and guidance on cross-domain systems point to the same conclusion: security built on fixed boundaries can no longer keep pace with how data actually moves.
File transfer is where that principle emerges most often in daily practice. Trust that was once given on principle must now be earned at every crossing. That shift, more than any single tool, is what will define resilient file transfer going forward.

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre warns that traditional file transfer systems are increasingly vulnerable, urging organizations to abandon perimeter-based trust in favor of proactive, continuous file verification.

### Key Points
- The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) warns that modern interconnected systems rely on outdated protocols that cannot withstand sophisticated cyberattacks.
- Traditional Managed File Transfer (MFT) models prioritize delivery speed over security, leaving organizations exposed to malware and supply chain vulnerabilities.
- High-profile incidents like the 2023 MoveIT breach demonstrate how attackers exploit the assumption that routine file transfer platforms are inherently safe.
- Security experts recommend deep content inspection, sandboxing, and Content Disarm and Reconstruction (CDR) to sanitize files before they enter internal networks.
- Organizations must shift from reactive patching to a security-first model where every file is validated at every stage of its journey.

### Why it Matters
Relying on perimeter-based security is no longer sufficient as attackers now exploit vulnerabilities within 48 hours of disclosure. By treating every file as a potential threat, businesses can prevent lateral movement and mitigate the risk of catastrophic data breaches in increasingly complex digital environments.
